newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Straits negotiator to attend HK handover - Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Straits negotiator to attend HK handover - Taiwan.

text.p: Taiwan said on Monday it would be represented at Hong Kong's June 30 handover by the head of a semi-official agency that handles the Nationalist island's recently deadlocked contacts with communist rival China.
Diplomats in Hong Kong predicted the gala midnight ceremony would present Taipei and Beijing with an attractive opportunity for some informal sideline talks.

"We have approved Straits Exchange Foundation chairman Koo Chen-fu to attend the events," said William Li, director of the Hong Kong and Macau affairs department of cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council.

Li said the foundation had sought permission for Koo to be in Hong Kong on June 30 to witness the lowering of the British flag and the raising of China's red five-star in a ceremony ending 156 years of British colonial rule.
No senior officials of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China were expected to attend.
Koo had said he expected to go, but an announcement in Hong Kong on Monday that 60 Taiwan people had been invited did not mention Koo by name or say who would head Taiwan's delegation.

The Mainland Affairs Council, Taiwan's top China policy planning body, supervises and finances the technically private Straits Exchage Foundation, which represents the island in talks with Beijing in the absence of formal ties.

Koo's expected presence raised the prospects that a meeting with his Beijing counterpart, Wang Daohan of the Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait, finally could take place -- two years after acute political hostilities and related military tensions scuttled a planned June 1995 meeting.
Koo's attendance at the gala will present prickly protocol problems for Hong Kong organisers.

Taipei -- whose Nationalist republic regards itself as the political equal of Beijing's communist People's Republic -- has said it would reject any seating arrangement that gave Taiwan the status of a mere province of China.
Yet organisers cannot accord Koo the same status given to a national representative.
Taipei and Beijing split in 1949 after a civil war that left the vast mainland in communist control and Taiwan in the hands of the defeated Chinese Nationalist government.
Beijing views the island as a renegade province and opposes any country according it diplomatic recognition.

Li of the Mainland Affairs Council appeared to give Hong Kong a bit of diplomatic wiggle room, saying Taiwan officials, lawmakers or prominent citizens could attend the gala events as long as they were "accorded with proper respect".

"We can accept arrangements in which our officials are treated as ordinary guests," Li said. "But it is totally unacceptable for our representatives to be seated with the mainland's provincial representatives."
Taiwan advocates eventual unification with the mainland but not before the ruling Communist Party gives up its political monopoly and introduces pluralism.
It adamantly rejects Beijing's proposal of reunification under a "one country, two systems" model of local autonomy that China says it will pioneer in Hong Kong from July 1.
Among the Taiwan people known to have been invited is Kao Chin-yen, leader of food giant President group and chairman of Taiwan's powerful National Chinese Federation of Industries.
Scholar Chen Yu-chun of Taipei's Chinese Culture University, who has a contract to teach at Beijing University for a year, told the United Daily News he also was invited.
